To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
self-focus leads to more helping when the helping request is salient and when the self is perceived to be responsible for the distressed other's welfare.
increasing self-focus will lead to an increase in helping behavior provided that the increase in helping is accompanied by an increase in felt responsibility for the other.
increasing self-focus will lead to increased helping behavior under conditions of high request salience, but not under conditions of low request salience.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the conditions under which increasing self-focus increases helping and the conditions under which it does not.
the role of self-focus, felt responsibility, and helping request salience in determining the likelihood of helping behavior.
the relationship between self-focused attention, felt responsibility, helping request salience and helping behavior.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the relationship between the self-focus and helping behaviors is not a simple one, but rather, is a complex function of the salience of the request for help and the individual's felt responsibility for the other.
self-focus, by itself, is neither necessary nor sufficient to produce helping behavior.
self-focus, by itself, does not lead to helping.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the effects of self-focus on helping behavior are not direct but are mediated by felt responsibility for the other.
self-focus is a necessary, but not sufficient, condition for helping behavior to occur.
helping behavior is a function of felt responsibility and that the relationship between felt responsibility and self-focus is mediated by salience of the request to help.
The main takeaway from our work is that
self-focus can lead to helping behavior only when it is accompanied by an increase in felt responsibility for the distress of the person in need.
self-focus does not necessarily lead to helping behavior, but that it can lead to increased helping if it is accompanied by an increased sense of responsibility for the distressed person.
self-focus can be a powerful predictor of helping.
